locations.name: Newcastle
locations.depot: Stock for the Hunter comes south down the Pacific Highway from our Grafton depot, with anything out of the ordinary carted from the Cornubia yard in south-east Queensland.
locations.leadTime: Usually 4–7 business days, scheduled around the southbound run
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft; crane truck for 40ft, for the old terrace streets and for any lift over a fence
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Newcastle and the Hunter. Delivery planned for terrace streets, harbour fill, Stockton sand and soft river flats.
locations.line: Nobody in Newcastle needs a container explained to them. The harbour handles them by the thousand, the industrial land at Mayfield and Kooragang was laid out around moving steel and coal, and half the trades in the city have worked around one at some point. That familiarity is worth something, because it means the conversation starts at the useful end. What still catches people out is the last hundred metres. The inner suburbs were surveyed for a horse and cart, the coastal end is dune sand, and a fair slice of the western suburbs sits over ground that was mined long before anybody built on it.
locations.uses: lock-up storage behind the terraces at Cooks Hill, Islington and Carrington where the back yard is four metres wide, plant and consumables storage across the industrial land at Mayfield, Cardiff, Beresfield and Thornton, site stores on the constant knockdown and infill work through Adamstown, New Lambton and Merewether, gear storage for the marine and boating trades around Carrington and Stockton, feed, fencing and machinery storage on the small holdings out through Paterson, Dungog and the Williams valley, and vineyard equipment kept dry and locked around Pokolbin, Lovedale and Rothbury
access: Newcastle splits into four kinds of delivery and it is worth knowing which one you are before ordering. The industrial belt is the easy one. Mayfield, Kooragang, Steel River, Cardiff, Beresfield and the Thornton estates were built for articulated vehicles, the surfaces are hardstand, and there is usually plant on site already. Those jobs are a phone call. The inner suburbs are the opposite. Cooks Hill, Carrington, Islington, Wickham, Hamilton and the older parts of Mayfield have terrace frontages on narrow streets with parking both sides, rear lanes barely wide enough for a ute, and a back yard that is reached through a gate a wheelbarrow was the design brief for. Plenty of those are still deliverable, but with a crane truck lifting from the street rather than a tilt-tray threading down the side. The third case is sand. Stockton, Fern Bay and the strip running north toward Anna Bay sit on dune sand, and dune sand looks like a road surface and carries almost nothing. A loaded rear axle will find that out on a nature strip in about two metres. The fourth is water and old workings. Out through Hexham, Tarro, Raymond Terrace, Maitland and the Hunter flats the soil is river silt and alluvium, which sets hard through a dry spell and turns to grease after a week of rain. Across a lot of Lake Macquarie, Cardiff, Wallsend and West Wallsend the ground has old coal workings under it, and while that rarely affects a delivery it is worth mentioning to us if your block has any known movement, because we would rather place the unit on the most stable part of the site than the most convenient one. Three photos settle most of it: the street from the middle of the road, the approach itself, and the ground where the container will end up.

sections.h: Coming down the highway, not out of a Newcastle yard
p: We will be straight about how a Newcastle container reaches you. It is carted down the Pacific Highway from the Grafton depot, or occasionally from the Cornubia yard further north, and it travels on a scheduled run rather than on a truck kept idling in the Hunter waiting for your order. That is why four to seven business days is the honest window and why we will not promise you tomorrow afternoon. What you get in exchange is that the run is regular and the container is chosen before it is loaded, so you are not taking whatever happened to be nearest the gate.

The practical upshot is planning. If you have a fixed date — a settlement, a site start, a removalist already booked, a shed being demolished — tell us at the enquiry rather than after you have ordered, and we will build the run around it. If your date is soft, say that too, because a flexible date can often slot into a truck that is already coming this way. The one thing that does not help anybody is finding out on the Thursday that the container was needed on the Monday.

sections.h: Ground that remembers what used to be under it
p: Newcastle ground changes character in the space of a few streets. Harbour-side land at Carrington, Wickham and parts of Mayfield is reclaimed fill with a long industrial history and a shallow water table. Stockton and Fern Bay are dune sand. The Hunter flats through Hexham and Maitland are river silt. The western suburbs sit over old collieries. A shipping container puts a serious point load into each of its four corners, and on every one of those ground types, dropping it straight onto turf means uneven settling within a season.

The fix is the same everywhere and it is cheap: hardwood sleepers or concrete pads under the four corners, bedded in and checked level both ways and across both diagonals. That spreads the load, keeps the floor clear of damp ground so air can move underneath, and keeps the frame square. A square frame is a frame whose doors still swing with one hand in ten years. If the block has a fall on it, put the door end at the high side. Tell us what the ground is at the quote — sand, fill, silt, clay or a proper slab — and the timber comes on the truck.

sections.h: Hire while it is temporary, buy when it is not
p: Newcastle runs on projects, and hire suits anything with a finish date attached. A knockdown-rebuild at Merewether, a site store while a fitout runs, household contents parked somewhere dry while a Hamilton semi gets underpinned, gear for a shutdown that lasts six weeks. You are not carrying an asset you will be trying to move on afterwards, and you are not the one arranging a truck at the end of it.

Buying wins the moment the timeframe goes open-ended. A permanent store on an industrial lot at Cardiff, a workshop out the back of an acreage block at Paterson, a lock-up on a vineyard that will still be doing the same job in fifteen years. Grade is the other half of that decision and it is worth a minute rather than a guess. Cargo-worthy units are inspected wind and watertight before they are loaded, which is the standard to ask for when the container lives outdoors and holds anything you would be annoyed to lose. The grades page sets out the differences properly. Tell us what is going inside and how long for, and we will point you at the right one rather than the dearest one.

faqs.q: My Cooks Hill terrace has no side access at all. Can you still deliver?
faqs.a: Usually, with a crane truck lifting from the street over the roof or the rear fence. It is routine work in the inner suburbs, where the house fills the block width and the only gate is a metre wide. What decides it is reach and clearance — how far the container has to travel horizontally, what it has to clear on the way, whether there are power or comms lines across the frontage, and whether the street is wide enough to set the outriggers without closing it. Photos from the footpath, from the back yard looking toward the street, and one looking straight up at the wires will let us answer quickly.

faqs.q: Does mine subsidence affect putting a container in at Cardiff or Wallsend?
faqs.a: Not usually for the delivery itself, but it is worth telling us about. Much of the western Newcastle and Lake Macquarie area sits over old coal workings and falls inside a declared subsidence district, and any approval question there is between you and Subsidence Advisory NSW rather than something we can answer for your street. What matters to us is whether your block has known movement or a spot that has settled before, because we will site the container on the most stable ground available and set it on pads rather than straight on the surface.

faqs.q: How long does delivery to Newcastle actually take?
faqs.a: Four to seven business days is the normal window. The container comes south from the Grafton depot on a scheduled run rather than sitting in a Hunter yard, so this is a planned delivery, not a same-day one. A crane booking, a unit that needs a lockbox or vents fitted, or a stretch of wet weather on soft ground will add a day or two. Give us your date at the enquiry and we will work the schedule around it.

faqs.q: Can I see the container before it turns up in Newcastle?
faqs.a: The yard you can walk around is at 51–55 Bromley Street, Cornubia, about half an hour south-east of Brisbane, which is not a realistic drive from the Hunter for most people. So the practical answer is photos of the actual unit on request, sent before delivery — corners, door end, roof and the internal floor, not stock images of something else. If you are heading north anyway, ring first and we will have the unit accessible when you arrive.

locations.name: Wollongong
locations.depot: Containers for the Illawarra run down from our Grafton depot on the coastal schedule, with the last leg through Sydney and down the motorway.
locations.leadTime: Usually 5–8 business days; northern-suburbs and escarpment drops are booked into a quiet part of the day
locations.truck: Tilt-tray where there is a straight run onto the block; crane truck for below-street houses, the northern villages and most 40ft work
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Wollongong and the Illawarra. Mount Ousley, Bulli Pass, below-street driveways and escarpment ground allowed for.
locations.line: There is not much flat ground in Wollongong and what there is has a house on it. The city is wedged onto a narrow shelf between the escarpment and the sea, which is lovely to live on and awkward to deliver to, because the streets follow contours rather than a grid and a great many houses sit below the level of the road they are addressed from. Add the grades a loaded truck has to negotiate to get here at all, and the Illawarra becomes a place where the access conversation happens before the price conversation, not after it.
locations.uses: trade and maintenance storage around the Port Kembla industrial area, Unanderra and Kembla Grange, board, wetsuit and dive gear storage in the northern villages where the garage was lost years ago, site stores on the steep rebuild blocks through Figtree, Mount Pleasant and Keiraville, materials and tool storage for the estate work at Kembla Grange, Calderwood and Tullimbah, dry storage for dairy and small holdings on the Jamberoo and Kangaroo Valley side, and household storage while a Thirroul or Austinmer cottage is lifted and rebuilt
access: Getting to the Illawarra is itself part of the job. Mount Ousley is the main freight descent and it is a serious grade with brake-check requirements and arrester beds for a reason; Bulli Pass is not a road a long combination has any business on. Neither stops us, but both mean an Illawarra run is planned around traffic and time of day rather than squeezed in. The northern villages are the tightest part of the district. Thirroul, Austinmer, Coledale, Scarborough and Stanwell Park hang off the escarpment on a single coastal road with hairpins, one-lane pinch points, blind driveways and mature figs overhanging at four metres. A 20ft on a tilt-tray gets up there. A 40ft is a conversation to have before you order rather than after. The signature Wollongong access problem, though, is the house below the road. Right through Figtree, Mount Keira, Mount Pleasant, Balgownie and Woonona the block falls away from the kerb, the driveway pitches down hard and the usable yard is ten or twelve metres below the truck. A tilt-tray cannot place a container downhill onto that; a crane truck can lower it, and that is what we book. Underfoot, the escarpment foothills are sandstone shelf and slipping clay in roughly equal measure — there are recognised landslip zones on those slopes, and a heavy stationary load in the wrong spot on the wrong slope is not something to guess at. The coastal flats at Windang, Warilla and Shellharbour are sand. The Dapto, Koonawarra and Albion Park flats are low ground on Mullet Creek and the Macquarie Rivulet that hold water for days. And the escarpment squeezes serious rain out of an east coast low, so wet-weather rescheduling here is normal rather than an excuse.

sections.h: The house is below the road
p: It is the most common Illawarra call we take. The address is fine, the street is fine, and the back yard is three metres below the driveway with a retaining wall between the two. A tilt-tray unloads by sliding a container rearwards down an inclined bed onto ground roughly level with the truck. It cannot place one at the bottom of a fall, and trying to reverse down a steep short drive with six metres of steel hanging past the rear axle ends with the bed grounding out on the kerb crest.

A crane truck solves it properly. It stands on the street, picks the container up and lowers it onto the lower ground, which turns an impossible job into a twenty-minute one. What it needs from you is information: how far down and how far across the container must travel, what is in between — roofline, pergola, palms, the neighbour's carport — and whether there are wires across the frontage. Reach falls away fast as the boom goes out, so eight metres over a fence and twenty metres over a two-storey house are different machines entirely. Stand at the gate and take three photos: down the drive, up at the lines, and from the yard looking back at the street.

sections.h: Rain, slope and where not to put it
p: The escarpment wrings rain out of anything coming in off the sea, and the Illawarra gets falls that flat country never sees. On a sloping block that changes where a container should sit. Water coming off the escarpment moves across blocks, not just down gutters, and a six-metre steel box parked square across an overland flow path will send that water somewhere the drainage was never designed for — usually against a wall or into the neighbour's yard.

The other half is what the container sits on. On a slope, build the low side up with stacked hardwood or set pads into the fall, rather than cutting a shelf into the high side. Cutting creates a trench that holds water against the bottom rail for the life of the unit. Building up keeps the underside open, keeps air moving and keeps all four corners at the same height, which is the only thing the frame actually cares about. Get that right and the doors keep swinging cleanly for decades. Get it wrong and the frame racks slowly, the doors start binding, and fixing it costs a great deal more than preventing it would have.

sections.h: Steel town storage, and whether to hire it
p: A lot of Illawarra container work is industrial and straightforward. A lock-up for tools and consumables on a leased lot at Unanderra or Kembla Grange, a store for spares that will not fit in the tenancy, a secure box for gear during a shutdown. Those deliveries are easy — the yards have hardstand, wide entries and room to work — so the only real decision is whether the container should be on your books or not.

Hire fits a lease with an end date, a project with a program, or a business that genuinely cannot say what it will need next winter. It also means the unit can be swapped for a bigger or smaller one if the job changes. Buying fits a permanent fixture on ground you control, and a bought 20ft holds value well here because there is real local demand for them second-hand. If it is going to live outside on the coast holding anything that must stay dry, ask for cargo-worthy — those units are inspected wind and watertight before loading. The grades page explains how the grades differ; tell us what is going inside and we will tell you which one you actually need.

faqs.q: How do you get a container up to Thirroul, Austinmer or Stanwell Park?
faqs.a: Along the coast road, carefully, and usually as a 20ft rather than a 40ft. That stretch is narrow with hairpins, pinch points, blind driveways and low canopy, and the length of the vehicle matters more than the weight. We book those drops for a quiet part of the day rather than into weekend beach traffic. If your requirement is genuinely 40ft of length up there, tell us early — two 20ft placed end to end often delivers more usable space and a far simpler delivery.

faqs.q: My Figtree yard is well below the street. Is that a problem?
faqs.a: It is normal here and it is the reason we ask about the drop before booking a truck. A tilt-tray cannot place a container onto ground below the road, so those jobs go on a crane truck that lowers the unit into the yard from the street. It works well provided we know the horizontal distance, the height it must clear and whether there are power lines across the frontage. Photos from the driveway and from the yard looking back up are the fastest way to get a straight answer.

faqs.q: Will wet weather push my Illawarra delivery back?
faqs.a: Sometimes, and we would rather ring you than bog a truck on your block. The escarpment pulls very heavy rain out of an east coast low, and the flats around Dapto, Koonawarra and Albion Park hold water long after the surface looks dry, while the escarpment slopes go greasy. On a hardstand industrial site rain barely matters. On a soft or sloping residential block, waiting two days beats a set of ruts across your yard and a tractor to get the truck out.

faqs.q: How long is delivery to Wollongong?
faqs.a: Five to eight business days is the normal window. Illawarra containers come down from the Grafton depot on a scheduled coastal run, so it is a planned delivery rather than a next-day one, and a crane booking or a northern-suburbs address can add a day. If you have a fixed date, tell us at the enquiry and we will build the run around it instead of telling you afterwards it did not fit.

locations.name: Tamworth
locations.depot: Tamworth stock is carted inland from our Grafton depot, up over the ranges and onto the New England, on a scheduled run rather than a truck kept waiting locally.
locations.leadTime: Usually 5–9 business days, built around the inland run
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for most town and property drops; crane truck where a gate, a yard or a set of powerlines makes a tilt unsafe
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Tamworth and the New England. Black soil, horse properties, long driveways and cattle grids planned for.
locations.line: Half the containers we send to Tamworth end up on a property with horses on it, and that changes how a delivery has to be run. The other half go to town blocks and to the sheds at Taminda, where the job is simpler. What links the two is the soil. Black soil is the best growing dirt in the country and the worst thing you can stand a heavy truck on after rain, and it does not give you much warning about which mode it is in. Getting the timing and the pad right is most of the work here.
locations.uses: hay, chaff and hard feed kept dry and away from vermin, tack, rugs and float gear stored properly instead of in the corner of a shed, vet supplies and drenches locked up out of the heat, fencing wire, posts and strainers in one place, trade storage on the industrial land at Taminda and Westdale, gear and materials for the constant build work at Calala, Hillvue and Moore Creek, and machinery parts and workshop tools on the cropping and grazing country out through Manilla, Kootingal, Nemingha and the Liverpool Plains
access: The first question on a Tamworth property delivery is what the driveway is made of and when it last rained. Black soil country does two things. In a dry spell it sets like a road, cracks open wide enough to lose a fencing tool down, and carries anything you put on it. Within an hour of decent rain the same surface turns to a grease that a loaded rigid truck will not climb, will not steer on, and will not stop on. There is no in-between and no way to tell from the house. That is why we ask, why we will move a booking by two days, and why the honest answer to a wet week is next week. The red basalt around Moore Creek and up toward Nundle behaves better but not by much. After that it is the usual property list, and every item on it is worth checking before you order. Cattle grids first: most private grids out here were built by a previous owner out of whatever rail was going, sized for a ute and a float, with no plate and no rating. A loaded truck is a different animal. If you do not know what the grid will take, say so and we will look at the side gate, a drop on firm ground near the road, or a crane lift instead. Then gates, which measure narrower at the swing than they look at the posts. Then culverts of unknown vintage on the driveway. Then turning space at the far end, which needs to be genuinely truck-sized, because a tilt-tray must line up straight to unload and nobody wants to reverse four hundred metres back to the road. And then the horses. A tilt bed unloading is loud — hydraulics, chains and a steel box sliding on a steel deck — so move stock out of the laneway and out of the paddock the truck has to pass through before we arrive, not while the driver is halfway down a drive with nowhere to turn.

sections.h: Working around an equine property
p: Tamworth has more horses per square kilometre than almost anywhere in the country, and a container delivery onto a working equine property is as much about the animals and the routine as it is about the ground. Tell us at the booking which gates have to stay shut behind us, which approach avoids the arena and the wash bays, whether anyone is working horses at the time we are due, and whether there is a preferred paddock lane. None of that is hard to plan for and all of it is impossible to fix once a truck is committed to a driveway.

It is also worth thinking about where the container earns its keep on that kind of place. Tack and rugs in a lockable steel box stay dry, stay out of the dust and stay away from mice. Hard feed keeps better and cannot be got at. Float gear, spare rails and the everything-else that accumulates around a horse operation ends up in one place instead of four sheds. Set it near the stables and the feed room rather than at the back of the block and you will use it every day.

sections.h: Black soil, cracks and getting it level
p: Vertosol black soil moves more than almost any other ground in Australia. It swells when it takes up water and shrinks hard as it dries, and it does not do either evenly across a paddock or a house block. Set a container straight onto it in October and by March one corner will have gone down and another up. The frame carries its whole load through four corners, and the moment those four points stop sitting at the same height the box works against itself, the frame racks, and the doors go from one-handed to a two-person shove.

Concrete pads or hardwood sleepers under the corners, bedded well and checked level in both directions and on both diagonals, deal with it. Make the pads bigger than you think on black soil, because the point of them is to spread load over a wider footprint than the casting itself. Keep the door end on the high side of any fall. Keep the underside clear and grass down so air moves through and water gets away. Do that once on delivery and it stays square, which on this country is not a given.

sections.h: Heat, dust and January
p: Two local realities worth planning around. The first is summer heat. A steel box in the open at Tamworth in January gets hot inside, and anything heat-sensitive — chemicals, some vet supplies, adhesives, electronics, anything with a temperature range printed on the label — needs to be thought about before it goes in. Vents help move air, siting it where it picks up afternoon shade helps more, and a light-coloured roof helps most. Fine western dust is the other constant, and it gets through any gap it can find, which is a good argument for a unit with sound door seals rather than the cheapest thing available.

The second is the festival. For ten days in January the town fills up, the roads are busy, accommodation is gone and getting a truck through the middle of Tamworth on a schedule is optimistic. If your container needs to be on the ground before or during that window, order well ahead of it. We would rather deliver a fortnight early than explain why a truck is sitting in traffic on Peel Street.

faqs.q: Will your truck cross the grid on my Tamworth property driveway?
faqs.a: That depends on the grid, and most private grids out here have no rating plate and no known history. A loaded truck carrying a container puts far more through it than the ute and float it was probably built for. If you know it is engineered and rated, tell us. If you do not, tell us that as well and we will look at a side gate, setting the container down on firm ground nearer the road for you to shift in with a tractor, or bringing a crane truck. All three beat finding out halfway across.

faqs.q: Can you deliver onto black soil after rain?
faqs.a: Not while it is wet, and we will say so rather than try. Black soil goes from concrete-hard to unusable within an hour of rain, and a loaded rigid truck on it will bog, chew a trench across the paddock or slide on a slope. We would rather ring you and move the day. If you have a hardstand near the road, a gravelled shed apron or a stretch of the drive that always stays firm, tell us — that is often the difference between delivering this week and waiting for the ground to dry out.

faqs.q: Is a container any good for storing feed and tack out here?
faqs.a: It is one of the main reasons people around Tamworth buy them. It is lockable, it keeps mice, birds and dust out far better than a shed with gaps, and cargo-worthy units are inspected wind and watertight before they are loaded, so what goes in dry stays dry. Two things make a difference: set it on pads so air moves under the floor rather than the floor sitting on damp ground, and open the doors on a dry day occasionally so any condensation clears rather than sitting in there through a humid spell.

faqs.q: How long will it take to get a container to Tamworth?
faqs.a: Five to nine business days is the usual window. Tamworth stock is carted inland from the Grafton depot, so it travels on a scheduled run rather than coming out of a local yard, and that is why we quote a window rather than a day. Wet ground, a crane booking, or the country festival week in January will all stretch it. If you have a fixed date — a shearing, a harvest, a shed being pulled down — give it to us at the enquiry and we will schedule to it.

locations.name: Dubbo
locations.depot: Dubbo containers travel west from our Grafton depot, and go onto the western schedule rather than a truck of their own.
locations.leadTime: Usually 6–10 business days, run with the western schedule
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for town blocks and firm property access; crane truck where the yard is tight or the ground will not take a truck close in
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Dubbo and the central west. Freight-town scheduling, red soil, river flats and real property access advice.
locations.line: Everything that moves across this state seems to turn at Dubbo. The Newell, the Mitchell and the Golden all meet here, the rail yards work through the night, and the town has built a genuine freight economy on being the place where the road changes direction. That works in your favour on scheduling, because a truck coming this way is a normal week rather than a special trip. It does not change the two things that actually decide the job: what your ground does when it is wet, and how much room a rigid truck has once it is through your gate.
locations.uses: hay, seed and chemical storage on the grazing and cropping country out through Wongarbon, Geurie, Narromine and Trangie, tool and plant storage across the industrial land at West Dubbo and along Boothenba Road, secure stores for the transport and logistics operators working the highway junctions, materials and site storage for the estate build work at Delroy, Keswick and Southlakes, gear storage for stock and station agents, contractors and shearing teams, and dry storage for tourism and accommodation operators around the zoo
access: Dubbo delivery divides on soil type, and the boundary is not obvious from the road. On the red-brown earths on the higher ground the surface holds up well, drains quickly and takes a truck without much complaint even a day after rain. On the grey and black cracking clays out on the Macquarie flats and west toward Narromine it is a different story: dry, it is as good as bitumen; wet, it is grease that a loaded rigid truck will not steer on, let alone climb. There is no middle setting, so the timing of the delivery matters more here than almost anything else about it. Long private driveways are the second factor. Two to four hundred metres of gravel with a crown and table drains either side is comfortable in the dry, and after a wet week the crown greases up and one wheel into the drain means a tractor. Grids are the third: most were built out of whatever rail the last owner had, sized for a ute and a float, and there is rarely a plate on them. Say so if you do not know, and we will drop on firm ground near the road or bring a crane truck instead. Then the ordinary details that stop a truck all the same. Gates narrower at the swing than at the posts. Powerlines running out to a pump shed or a silo, at exactly the wrong height for a raised tilt bed. Old ironbarks and kurrajongs with limbs at four metres. Turning space at the far end that has to be real, because a tilt-tray needs to be lined up straight before it unloads and four hundred metres of reversing is nobody's afternoon. In town, the older grid streets around West Dubbo and the CBD fringe are workable but have kerbside parking, mature street trees and short driveways, and the newer estates on the edges bring narrow carriageways, service pits at the kerb line and fill that has not had a summer on it yet.

sections.h: A freight town is easier to schedule for
p: Dubbo has one real advantage over most inland towns: it is on the way to everywhere. The road network converges here, so a container heading west from the Grafton depot is on a run that would exist anyway rather than a dedicated trip made for one order. That is what keeps a six to ten business day window realistic instead of a fortnight, and it is why a flexible delivery date is worth something to you. If you can take the container in a window rather than on a named day, tell us — it often slots into a truck already coming this way.

The other side is that we will not pretend to a same-week turnaround we cannot make. Dubbo is a road run from the eastern seaboard, not a local yard job, and anyone promising you tomorrow is either guessing or has already loaded something for somebody else. If you have a hard date — a lease starting, a shed coming down, a contractor arriving — give it to us at the enquiry, and we will tell you honestly whether it fits the schedule.

sections.h: Heat, dust and what goes inside
p: Summers out here are long and hot, and the inside of a closed steel box in a Dubbo February gets a lot hotter than the shade temperature. That is fine for machinery, steel, fencing gear, furniture and most of what people store. It is not fine for chemicals with a stated temperature range, some vet and animal health products, adhesives, paints, aerosols or anything electronic left in there through a summer. Whirlybirds or side vents move air through and make a real difference, and so does putting the container where it picks up afternoon shade rather than full western sun.

Dust is the other constant. Fine western dust will find any gap in a seal and settle on everything inside over a season. It is a good reason to spend the extra on a unit with sound door gaskets rather than the cheapest available, particularly if the contents are tools, feed or anything with a bearing in it. Cargo-worthy units are inspected wind and watertight before loading, and that same seal integrity is what keeps the dust out as well as the rain.

sections.h: The river, and where the container should sit
p: The Macquarie has come up over the flats more than once in recent memory, and people out here need no lecture on it. What is worth being plain about is what a container does and does not do. It is a very good store. It is not a flood barrier. Water reaching the door sill will get past the seals, and an empty container is a large sealed box that will lift and move if the water gets deep enough. Anybody selling you one on the strength of the water staying out is selling you something they should not.

So the useful conversation is siting. Put it on the highest usable part of the block rather than the flattest. Keep it out of the overland flow path, because a lot of damage on these flats comes from water running across country rather than from the river itself. If it is going to be a long-term store on low ground, set it up on blocks or a raised pad so the floor sits well clear and the underside stays dry and ventilated. Height is worth more than any other decision you will make about it.

faqs.q: Can you deliver out to a property at Narromine, Trangie or Wellington?
faqs.a: Yes, and those runs go on the same western schedule as Dubbo itself. What we need to know is the state of the driveway, whether there is a grid and what it is rated for, gate widths at the narrowest point, and whether there is real turning space at the far end. On the black soil flats we also need to know when it last rained. Where the drive is doubtful, dropping the container on firm ground near the road for you to shift in with a tractor is a perfectly good answer and often the fastest one.

faqs.q: Why is delivery to Dubbo measured in a window rather than a day?
faqs.a: Because the container is carted west from our Grafton depot on a scheduled run rather than sitting in a yard here. Six to ten business days is the honest range, and it is shorter when your date is flexible enough to fit an existing run. A crane booking, wet ground on the clay country or a unit needing vents or a lockbox fitted will push it out. Tell us your date at the enquiry and we will say straight away whether it works.

faqs.q: Is a container a sensible place to store chemicals and animal health products out here?
faqs.a: For most farm chemicals and general supplies, yes — it is lockable, it keeps stock and children out, and it keeps dust and weather off. The catch is heat. A closed steel container in a Dubbo summer runs well above ambient, and anything with a storage temperature on the label needs shade, ventilation, or a different home. Vents help, siting for afternoon shade helps more. Follow the label rather than our advice on the specific product, but plan the airflow before delivery rather than after.

faqs.q: Can I inspect the container before it comes to Dubbo?
faqs.a: The walk-around yard is at 51–55 Bromley Street, Cornubia in south-east Queensland, which is not a practical drive from the central west. What we do instead is send photos of the actual unit on request, before delivery — the corners, the door end, the roof and the internal floor, so you are looking at the container you are getting rather than a stock photo. Ask for them at the quote and they come with it.

locations.name: Wagga Wagga
locations.depot: Riverina orders come down the inland route from our Grafton depot and are scheduled onto the southern run.
locations.leadTime: Usually 7–12 business days, scheduled onto the southern run
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for town blocks, industrial yards and firm farm access; crane truck where a yard is tight or the container has to go over something
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Wagga Wagga and the Riverina. Frost, river flats, defence-base access and honest lead times on the southern run.
locations.line: Wagga is a good town to deliver to and a long way to deliver from. The road in is easy — the Sturt and the Olympic Highway feed straight into a town laid out with room in it, and the industrial land at Bomen was built around rail and freight, so heavy vehicles are not a novelty. The distance is the honest constraint. This is a scheduled southern run, not a truck sitting at Bomen waiting on your order, and the two local factors that then decide the job are the river flats and the cold.
locations.uses: grain, seed and chemical storage on the cropping country out through Coolamon, Junee and Lockhart, wool and shearing gear kept dry between sheds, plant and consumables storage across the Bomen and East Wagga industrial estates, site stores for the build work at Estella, Boorooma and Gobbagombalin, secure storage for contractors working the defence establishments, machinery and irrigation parts on the river flats country, and household storage while a North Wagga or Turvey Park place is renovated
access: Wagga is generous with space by inland-town standards, and most of the industrial and rural work here is straightforward. Bomen, East Wagga and the freight precinct were laid out for articulated vehicles and have hardstand, wide entries and room to swing, and a delivery into one of those is about as simple as it gets. The complications are elsewhere. The Murrumbidgee flats — North Wagga, Gumly Gumly, Oura and the low country either side of the river — are alluvial silt and sandy loam, which is beautiful ground to farm and unreliable ground to park twenty tonne on after rain. It sets firm through a dry spell, then holds water below a surface that looks dry, and a rear axle will find the soft layer. The same soil under a long farm driveway makes the difference between an easy run in and a tractor. Winter adds two things you do not get further north. Heavy frost lifts and softens a surface overnight, so a driveway that carried a truck at four in the afternoon can be greasy at eight the next morning, and we will often book a mid-morning slot for that reason alone. Thick river fog can hold a start time back as well. In town, the older streets through Turvey Park, Kooringal and Ashmont have short driveways, established street trees and side gates set out narrower than a modern truck wants, while the newer estates north of the river bring the familiar pattern of narrow carriageways, cars parked both sides and service pits on the kerb line that will crack under a loaded rear axle. Deliveries onto the defence establishments are their own category: they need gate approval, a named contact, an induction in some cases and a booked window, and all of that is easy a week out and impossible on the morning.

sections.h: Cold country and condensation
p: A steel container in a frosty climate does something people from warmer parts never see. On a clear winter night the shell drops below the dew point of the air trapped inside, moisture condenses on the underside of the roof, and by morning it drips. Store cardboard cartons, upholstery, feed sacks, hay or anything with paper on it under that and you will find damp patches that have nothing to do with a leak in the roof. It is the single most common complaint we hear from cold-climate customers and it is entirely preventable.

The fixes are simple and cheap. Vents at both ends let air move through so humid air is not sealed in overnight. Getting the unit off the ground on pads stops ground moisture wicking up into the space. Loading dry, leaving a gap between stacked goods and the walls, and putting a couple of moisture absorbers in for a winter all help. For a conversion or anything needing a stable interior — a workshop, an office, a store for anything sensitive — insulating the ceiling is what actually solves it, because it stops the steel getting cold enough to sweat in the first place.

sections.h: The river flats and the levee
p: Everybody in Wagga knows where the water goes and roughly how high it gets, so we will stick to the container end of it. A container is a good store and a poor barrier. Water that reaches the door sill will get past the seals, and an empty container floats — it will lift, drift and end up somewhere you did not put it if the water gets deep enough. That is not a reason to avoid one on the flats. It is a reason to site it deliberately.

On low ground, height is the only thing doing real work. Put the unit on the highest usable part of the block rather than the most convenient one, keep it out of the overland flow path, and set it on blocks or a raised pad so the floor sits well clear of the ground. That has the useful side effect of keeping the underside ventilated and dry year-round, which matters on silt that stays damp. If you are storing anything irreplaceable, treat height as the decision that counts and everything else as detail.

sections.h: Ordering ahead of the season
p: Riverina demand runs on a calendar. Storage gets wanted before harvest, before shearing, before a contractor starts, and everyone wants it in the same fortnight. Since Wagga containers travel down on a scheduled run rather than sitting in a local yard, the seven to twelve business day window is real and the way to beat it is to order ahead of the rush rather than during it. A month's notice before harvest gets you the size and grade you asked for. Three days' notice gets you whatever is already loaded.

Hire is worth a look where the need has an end date on it — a season, a build, a lease, a shed being replaced after a storm. Buying makes sense where the container becomes part of how the place runs, and out here they generally do. If it is going to live in the open holding grain, seed, feed, tools or anything that must stay dry, ask for cargo-worthy, which is inspected wind and watertight before it is loaded. The grades page sets out what separates the grades so you can pick on facts rather than on price alone.

faqs.q: Why does my container sweat inside during a Wagga winter?
faqs.a: Because the steel drops below the dew point overnight and the moisture in the trapped air condenses on the roof and runs down. It is condensation, not a leak, and it is normal in a frost climate. Vents at both ends, the unit up on pads so ground moisture is not wicking in, loading everything dry with a gap to the walls, and moisture absorbers over winter will handle most of it. For a workshop or anything sensitive, insulating the ceiling stops it at the source.

faqs.q: Can you deliver onto RAAF Wagga or Kapooka?
faqs.a: Yes, but those deliveries have to be arranged rather than simply booked. Base access typically means a gate pass, a named contact expecting the vehicle, a nominated window and sometimes an induction for the driver, and none of that can be organised at the boom gate on the day. Get the approval and the window in hand, tell us what the requirements are at the booking, and we will schedule the run to land inside it.

faqs.q: Why is delivery to Wagga slower than the coast?
faqs.a: Distance and honesty. The container is carted from our Grafton depot on a scheduled southern run rather than sitting in a Riverina yard, so seven to twelve business days is the realistic window. Frost, fog and wet ground on the river flats can shift a booking by a morning or a day. If you have a hard date, tell us before you order and we will say plainly whether it fits rather than agreeing and disappointing you later.

faqs.q: What size suits a Riverina farm store?
faqs.a: A 20ft covers most of it — seed, chemical, tools, shearing gear, a bench along one side — and it is much easier to get down a farm driveway and through a gate than the alternative. A 40ft gives you machinery-length storage and suits a working shed area with a straight approach off a formed road. Where the driveway is tight but you want the volume, two 20ft set with a gap between them and a roof across the middle is a very common Riverina setup and gives you covered hardstand into the bargain.

locations.name: Albury
locations.depot: Border orders come down the inland route from our Grafton depot and are scheduled onto the same southern run as the Riverina.
locations.leadTime: Usually 7–12 business days on the southern schedule
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for most town, estate and industrial drops; crane truck for tight yards, over-fence lifts and awkward river-block access
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Albury, Wodonga and along the Murray. Cross-border realities, frost, river flats and honest delivery windows.
locations.line: Albury is one address and two sets of rules. The Murray runs through the middle of it, the state line runs with the river, and a container going into a Lavington back yard and the same container going into a Wodonga back yard are answerable to different councils even though the two blocks are ten minutes apart. That is worth knowing before you order rather than after. The road side is comparatively kind: the Hume runs straight past, the freight and rail precinct north of town is built for heavy vehicles, and access is rarely the hard part.
locations.uses: trade and plant storage across the industrial and rail freight land north of town and out toward Ettamogah, materials and site storage for the estate build work at Thurgoona and Springdale Heights, stock, feed and fencing storage on the grazing and cropping country through Jindera, Walla Walla, Howlong and Culcairn, gear storage for the manufacturing and food processing businesses on both sides of the river, boat and camping gear kept locked up near the Murray and Lake Hume, and household storage while an East Albury or North Albury place is being worked on
access: Albury does not throw many hard access problems, and where it does they cluster in three places. The first is the river country. Blocks running down toward the Murray and along the anabranches at Thurgoona, Table Top and out toward Howlong sit on sandy river loam and old flood deposits between stands of river red gum. That soil drains fast, looks solid and softens under a rear axle without much warning, and the big gums drop limbs and hang low enough over a track to catch a raised tilt bed. The second is the hill country on the western edge — Nail Can and the ridges behind West Albury — where granite outcrops mean short, steep driveways with rock ledge under them, so the block is firm but very rarely level. That is a good problem to have, provided we know before we send a tilt-tray to a driveway that pitches away at the kerb. The third is winter mornings. Frost is heavy here from May through August and it lifts a surface overnight, so a gravel driveway or a paddock track that carried a truck yesterday afternoon can be greasy at eight this morning, and river fog can hold a start back an hour or two. We will often book a mid-morning slot on rural addresses through winter for exactly that reason. Around town, the older streets in East and North Albury have short pitched driveways, mature street trees and narrow side gates, while the newer estates at Thurgoona and Springdale Heights bring the standard estate list: tight carriageways, cars parked both sides, service pits and stormwater grates on the kerb line that a loaded axle will crack, and cut-and-fill blocks with thin turf over ground that has not settled. Photos from the street and of the spot itself sort nearly all of it out before a truck leaves.

sections.h: Two states, one town
p: The border is the local peculiarity you cannot ignore. Albury sits in New South Wales, Wodonga in Victoria, and the two councils take their own view on how long a container can stay on a residential block, whether it can be seen from the street, and what happens if you alter it. Newer estates on either side may add a covenant on top that is stricter again. We are not going to guess at the rule for your street, and anybody who tells you the answer without asking which side of the river you are on is not paying attention.

What is consistent is the shape of the question. Is it temporary or permanent. Is it visible from the road. Is it storage or a conversion. Does the estate or body corporate have anything to say. Sort that before delivery, because moving a container twenty metres after the fact is a second delivery, not an adjustment. Sited behind the building line, screened by a fence or planting, level and clear of a drainage path keeps almost everybody comfortable regardless of which state you are in.

sections.h: Frost, fog and a sweating roof
p: Albury gets proper winters, and a sealed steel box in a frost climate collects moisture on the inside of its roof overnight. The air inside cools, the moisture in it condenses on the coldest surface, and by morning it drips. People blame the roof. It is almost never the roof. Cartons go soft, tools spot with surface rust and anything with paper on it takes up damp, all without a drop of rain getting in.

It is easy to design out. Vents at each end so air moves through instead of sitting. Pads under the corners so the floor is not in contact with damp ground wicking moisture upward. Load dry, leave a gap between the stack and the walls so air can circulate around it, and run a couple of moisture absorbers through the coldest months. If you are converting the container into a workshop, an office or a store for anything that needs a stable environment, insulate the ceiling — that keeps the steel above dew point and stops the problem happening rather than managing it afterwards.

sections.h: Reaching the smaller towns
p: A lot of what we send to the Albury area does not stop in Albury. Jindera, Howlong, Corowa, Holbrook, Culcairn, Walla Walla, Henty and the properties in between are all part of the same run, and because those addresses are already off the highway the extra distance matters much less than the last few hundred metres does. What we need for a property drop is the same short list every time: the state of the driveway and when it last rained, whether there is a grid and what it might carry, the gate width at its narrowest, and whether there is genuinely truck-sized turning space at the far end.

Where any of that is doubtful, setting the container down on firm ground near the road and letting you walk it in with a tractor at your own pace is a perfectly respectable answer and often the quickest. A crane truck standing near the road can also place a unit further in than a tilt-tray could reach. Both beat committing a loaded truck to a driveway it cannot back out of, which is the one outcome nobody recovers a good day from.

faqs.q: Do the rules differ for a container in Albury versus Wodonga?
faqs.a: They can, and that is the thing to check before you order rather than afterwards. Albury sits under a New South Wales council and Wodonga under a Victorian one, and they take their own positions on how long a container can stay, whether it is visible from the road and whether it has been altered. Estate covenants add another layer on either side. We will not guess at your street. The reliable pattern is that temporary, screened and used for storage is the easy end, and permanent, prominent and modified is where questions start.

faqs.q: How long does a container take to reach Albury?
faqs.a: Seven to twelve business days is the honest window. Border deliveries come down from our Grafton depot on a scheduled southern run rather than out of a local yard, so this is a planned delivery and we would rather tell you that up front than promise a date we would miss. Winter frost, fog and wet rural driveways can shift a booking by a morning. Give us your date at the enquiry and we will tell you straight away whether it fits the schedule.

faqs.q: Will a container be alright sitting under river red gums on a Murray block?
faqs.a: The container will. The delivery needs thought, because those gums hang low over tracks and drop limbs without much notice, and a tilt-tray needs vertical clearance for a raised bed rather than just enough room to drive under. Once it is in place, keep leaf litter swept off the roof — wet leaves held against a panel are what starts surface corrosion, far more than weather does — and keep the grass down around the base so moisture is not trapped against the steel.

faqs.q: Can I get photos of the container before it is sent down?
faqs.a: Yes, and on a run this length it is the sensible thing to do. Ask at the quote and we will send photos of the actual unit on request before delivery — the corners, the door end, the roof and the internal floor, so there is nothing to argue about when the truck arrives. The walk-around yard is at Cornubia in south-east Queensland, which is not a realistic trip from the border for most people.

locations.name: Orange
locations.depot: Central west orders are carted inland from our Grafton depot and go onto the scheduled tablelands run.
locations.leadTime: Usually 6–10 business days; winter drops on unsealed ground are booked for later in the morning
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for town blocks, orchards and firm farm tracks; crane truck for tight yards and where a truck cannot get close to the spot
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Orange and district. Cold-climate condensation, basalt soil, orchard and vineyard access and honest lead times.
locations.line: Orange sits high enough that the weather is a genuine part of the specification, not small talk. Frost most of winter, snow on Canobolas some years, and cold clear nights that make a steel box sweat on the inside if nobody has thought about ventilation. Then there is the soil, which is the deep red basalt that grows the apples and the cherries and holds water like a sponge through a long wet winter. Both of those change what you should buy and how the delivery has to be timed, and both are easier to deal with before the truck is booked.
locations.uses: bin, netting and irrigation gear storage on the orchards through Nashdale, Borenore and Spring Hill, vineyard equipment and harvest gear kept dry and locked, contractor and maintenance storage for the mining and services businesses working out of the district, trade storage on the industrial land around Leewood and the northern distributor, hay, fencing and stock gear on the grazing country through Molong, Cargo and Lucknow, site stores on the newer build work at Clifton Grove and North Orange, and household storage while a period cottage in the older streets is renovated
access: The basalt country around Orange is the best growing soil in the state and it holds water for weeks. Through a wet winter a paddock track or an orchard row that carried a tractor all summer will not carry a loaded rigid truck, and the damage a bogged truck does to a working orchard is worse than the delay would have been. That is the main reason we push a booking here rather than the main reason we cancel one, and it is why winter deliveries onto unsealed ground get booked for later in the morning once the frost has come out and gone off. Frost is the second factor and it works both ways: hard frost sets a surface overnight and makes it excellent at seven in the morning, then thaws it into grease by nine. On the higher ground toward Canobolas there is snow some winters and it is rarely deep enough to matter, but ice on a steep unsealed drive matters a great deal. Then the ground itself. Basalt is heavy clay that swells and shrinks through the year, so a container set straight onto it will move with the seasons and go out of square. Where the basalt gives way to granite around the district you get the opposite: firm as anything, rarely level, and occasionally a ledge just under the surface that stops a peg going in where you wanted the pad. In town, the older streets around the CBD, Glenroi and Bletchington have short driveways, mature exotic street trees that were planted well before anyone imagined a twelve-metre truck, and narrow side gates. Orchard and vineyard properties bring long tracks, gates set at an angle to the road, headland turning space that is sized for a tractor rather than a rigid, and low wires running out to pump sheds and cool rooms. None of it is difficult if we know first.

sections.h: The cold makes containers sweat
p: This is the single most useful thing to know about a container in a cold-climate town, and it is the thing least often mentioned when one is sold. On a clear Orange night the steel drops well below the dew point of the air sealed inside. Moisture condenses on the underside of the roof and by morning it is dripping. Cartons soften, tools spot, and anything with paper or fabric in it takes up damp. Every year somebody rings believing the roof leaks. It almost never does.

Design it out at the start. Vents at both ends so air moves rather than sits. Pads under the corners so ground moisture is not wicking up into the space. Load everything dry, leave a gap between the stack and the walls so air circulates around it, and put a couple of moisture absorbers in over winter. If the container is becoming a workshop, an office, a cellar-door store or anything else that needs a stable interior, insulate the ceiling — that keeps the steel above dew point and removes the problem instead of managing it every July.

sections.h: Setting one on basalt
p: Red basalt clay is generous soil and difficult footing. It takes up an enormous amount of water through winter and gives it back through summer, swelling and shrinking as it goes, and it does not do it evenly under a six-metre footprint. Set a container straight onto it in February and by August one corner has settled and another has lifted. The frame carries its entire load through the four corners, so once those stop sitting at the same height the box starts working against itself, the frame racks and the doors go from a one-hand job to a shove.

Concrete pads or hardwood sleepers under the corners fix it, and on this soil make them larger than you would elsewhere — the whole point is to spread the load over more ground than the casting itself covers. Bed them properly, check level in both directions and across both diagonals, and put the door end on the high side of any fall so the doors swing with gravity instead of against it. Keep the underside open so water can get away and air can move, which on ground that stays wet for months is worth as much as the levelling.

sections.h: Orchard, vineyard and mine-services work
p: The district's container work has a distinct local flavour. Orchards want bin storage, netting, irrigation fittings and spray gear locked up and dry between seasons. Vineyards want the same for harvest equipment and hoses. The mining and services businesses want secure, weatherproof stores that can be shifted when a contract moves. Every one of those is a good use for a container, and every one of them has the same two requirements: it has to stay dry inside and it has to be able to be moved later.

Both come back to setup rather than to the container. A unit that has bedded itself into wet basalt over five years has to be dug out before a truck can lift it, whereas one sitting on pads comes straight up. If it lives outdoors holding anything that must stay dry, ask for cargo-worthy — those units are inspected wind and watertight before they are loaded. The grades page goes through what separates one grade from another, so you can choose on what you are storing rather than on the number at the bottom of the quote.

faqs.q: Does snow or frost cause problems for a container at Orange?
faqs.a: Not for the container itself. The steel is unbothered, and the light snow the district gets most winters clears on its own. What frost changes is the ground and the timing: a driveway that is rock hard at seven in the morning is grease by nine as the thaw comes out of it, so we book winter deliveries onto unsealed ground for mid-morning. The other cold-weather issue is inside — condensation on the roof overnight — which vents, pads and a bit of airflow will handle, or insulation if you are converting it.

faqs.q: Can you get a container down an orchard or vineyard row at Nashdale or Borenore?
faqs.a: Sometimes, and it depends more on the season than the row. Through summer the tracks are firm and it is usually straightforward. Through a wet winter the basalt holds water and a loaded truck will bog and tear a working block up, which costs you more than waiting would. Headland turning space is the other constraint, since a tilt-tray must line up straight to unload. Where the row is doubtful, we will set the container on firm ground near the shed for you to move in with a tractor.

faqs.q: How long is delivery to Orange?
faqs.a: Six to ten business days is the usual window. Containers for the central west are carted inland from the Grafton depot on a scheduled run rather than sitting in a yard here, so it is a planned delivery rather than a next-day one. Winter ground conditions and crane bookings can add a day or two. If you have a fixed date — a harvest, a contractor starting, a shed coming down — tell us at the enquiry and we will schedule around it.

faqs.q: What can I do about damp getting into stored goods over winter?
faqs.a: Treat it as a ventilation problem rather than a waterproofing one. Fit vents at both ends, set the container up on pads so it is not sitting on damp ground, load everything bone dry, leave an air gap between the stack and the walls, and use moisture absorbers through the coldest months. Pallets under boxes rather than boxes on the floor makes a real difference too. For anything genuinely sensitive, insulating the ceiling stops the roof reaching dew point in the first place.

locations.name: Bathurst
locations.depot: Bathurst orders travel inland from our Grafton depot and are scheduled onto the same tablelands run as the rest of the central west.
locations.leadTime: Usually 6–10 business days; avoid the week of the October race meeting
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for town blocks, industrial yards and firm rural access; crane truck where the yard is tight or the spot cannot be reached directly
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Bathurst, Kelso and district. Frost hollows, granite country, race-week scheduling and cold-climate condensation.
locations.line: Two things shape a Bathurst delivery and neither of them is the container. The first is cold. This is a frost hollow on a plain at nine hundred metres, the fog sits in it on winter mornings, and a sealed steel box in that climate will collect water on the inside of its roof unless somebody has thought about airflow. The second is one week in October, when the town's population multiplies, every road in is busy and a truck on a schedule is optimistic. Plan around both and the rest of the job is comparatively simple.
locations.uses: hay, feed and fencing storage on the grazing country out through Perthville, Rockley and O'Connell, tool and materials storage on the industrial land at Kelso and Raglan, site stores for the estate build work at Kelso, Eglinton and Windradyne, timber and milling gear storage around Oberon, gear storage for motorsport, car clubs and event operators who need everything locked away for eleven months of the year, machinery parts and workshop storage on small holdings through Sofala and Wattle Flat, and household storage while a heritage cottage in the older streets is worked on
access: Bathurst town is easier than most inland centres because the older streets were laid out wide, so a rigid truck can generally stand where it needs to. The constraints sit around the edges. The heritage streets near the centre have short pitched driveways, verandah posts and awnings close to the footpath, mature exotic street trees with low limbs, and side gates set out long before a modern truck existed — plenty of those are crane jobs rather than tilt jobs. The newer estates at Kelso, Eglinton and Windradyne bring the standard pattern: narrow carriageways, cars parked both sides, stormwater grates and service pits on the kerb line that a loaded rear axle will crack, and cut-and-fill blocks with thin turf over young ground that has not been through enough wet and dry cycles to settle. Out of town it is granite and cold. The granite country gives firm footing and almost no level ground, and there is often rock ledge just under the surface, which is excellent for bearing a load and inconvenient when you want a pad set exactly where you planned it. Frost is the real scheduling factor. Hard frost sets a paddock track solid overnight and then thaws it to grease through the morning, so a winter delivery onto unsealed ground gets booked for a sensible hour rather than first thing, and heavy fog on the plain can hold a start back regardless. The Macquarie flats through town and downstream hold water and stay soft after rain. Approaches from the east come over the Great Western and the descent off the range is a genuine grade for a loaded truck, which is one more reason a Bathurst run is planned rather than squeezed in at the end of a day.

sections.h: Race week is a real constraint
p: For one week in October the town does something no other regional centre in the state does. The population multiplies several times over, the approaches fill up, accommodation disappears and the local road network runs at a level it was never built for. A container truck trying to keep a delivery schedule through that week is not a plan, it is a hope. We say this plainly because people forget until it is on top of them.

If you want a container on the ground for the event — extra secure storage for a club, a team, a camping group, a vendor or a property being used for the week — order it well ahead and take delivery a fortnight early. It costs nothing to have it sitting there and it removes the one variable you cannot control. The same goes in reverse: if you are storing gear away afterwards, a booking a week or two after the event is a much smoother run than one made in the middle of it.

sections.h: A frost hollow and what it does inside the box
p: Bathurst is famously cold on a clear winter night and a shipping container responds to that in a way people are rarely warned about. The shell drops below the dew point of the air sealed inside, moisture condenses along the underside of the roof and drips. Boxes go soft, tools show surface rust, fabric and paper take up damp, and it all looks exactly like a leaking roof to anyone who has not seen it before.

It is straightforward to prevent. Vents at both ends so air moves through rather than sitting still. Pads under the four corners so the floor is not in contact with cold damp ground. Load everything dry, keep an air gap between the stack and the walls, use pallets rather than putting cartons straight on the floor, and run moisture absorbers through the winter months. If the container is becoming a workshop, a hobby space or a store for anything sensitive, insulate the ceiling. That keeps the steel above dew point and ends the problem rather than managing it every winter.

sections.h: Granite, slope and levelling it once
p: Very little ground around Bathurst is naturally level, and a container does not need it to be. What it needs is four corners at the same height. On a slope, build the low side up with stacked hardwood or set pads into the fall. Do not cut a shelf out of the high side — that creates a channel that holds water against the bottom rail for the life of the unit, which is the one thing you do not want on cold, wet ground.

Granite country actually makes this easier once you find your levels, because the bearing is excellent and the pads will not sink into it. What it does mean is that where you want a pad and where the rock lets you have one are not always the same place, so we set out on site rather than to a drawing. Put the door end on the high side so the doors swing with gravity, keep the underside open so air moves and water drains away, and check it is square across both diagonals before the truck leaves. Done once on delivery, it stays that way for decades.

faqs.q: Can you deliver during Bathurst race week in October?
faqs.a: We would rather not, and we will tell you why honestly. That week the approaches and the local roads carry many times their normal traffic, and a truck on a delivery schedule cannot be relied on to arrive when it said it would. If you need a container in place for the event, order early and take it a fortnight before. If you are storing gear afterwards, book a week or two after everything has cleared out. Either way you get a delivery that runs to time.

faqs.q: Does the frost cause any problem for a container at Bathurst?
faqs.a: Not to the steel. It changes two other things. On the ground, a hard frost sets a paddock track or a gravel drive solid overnight then thaws it to grease through the morning, so we book winter drops onto unsealed ground for later in the day rather than first thing. Inside, cold clear nights cause condensation on the underside of the roof, which people often mistake for a leak. Vents, pads under the corners and dry loading handle it, and ceiling insulation stops it entirely if you are converting the unit.

faqs.q: There is rock just under the surface where I want it. Does that matter?
faqs.a: It is generally good news. Granite ledge gives you excellent bearing and pads set on rock will not sink, which is more than can be said for a lot of soils. The practical issue is placement — you may not be able to put a pad exactly where you planned if there is rock in the way, so we set out on site rather than to a fixed measurement. The rule stays the same regardless: four corners at the same height, door end on the high side, underside kept open.

faqs.q: How long does a container take to get to Bathurst?
faqs.a: Six to ten business days is the normal window. Containers for the central west are carted inland from our Grafton depot on a scheduled run rather than sitting in a local yard, which is why we quote a window rather than a day. Winter ground conditions, a crane booking or the October event week will push it out. Tell us your date at the enquiry and we will confirm honestly whether that fits the schedule.
